10600-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels gathers accounts of discovery into a vast survey, and this first volume covers the Middle Ages. It opens with Norse voyages to Iceland, the travels of Ohthere to the White Sea and the Baltic, and early journeys toward India. A general plan divides the whole set from King Alfred's age to the scientific voyages of George III.

The volume mixes sailors' reports, notes on geography, and short histories of how navigation grew. Readers follow step by step as Europeans learned the shape of the seas around them. The book suits anyone curious about exploration before the great age of ocean voyages.
10803-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels reaches its second volume in this 1824 Edinburgh edition, illustrated with maps and charts. The volume continues early pilgrimages from England to the Holy Land between 1097 and 1107, then tells of Madeira and the conquest of the Canary Islands. Its second part opens the Portuguese discoveries from Prince Henry in 1412.

Kerr arranges voyages in systematic order, forming a complete history of navigation, discovery, and commerce by sea and land. The volume suits readers tracing Europe's slow learning of the oceans. It preserves early travel accounts in a clear, scholarly frame.
12325-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr published this third volume of A General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels in Edinburgh and London in 1824, illustrated by maps and charts. Kerr, a fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, arranged voyages in systematic order as a complete history of navigation, discovery, and commerce.

Volume three covers voyages by sea and land from the earliest ages to Kerr day. A mid-book passage treats Italian towns and the Columbi families of Cucaro and Placentia, granted lands by an emperor in 940. The collection draws on Hakluyt, Purchas, and other sources, edited into a continuous narrative. It remains a useful early reference for exploration history, though modern scholars check its texts against originals.
12330-a-volunteer-poilu:
Henry Sheahan published A Volunteer Poilu as a memoir of service in France during the First World War. Sheahan dedicates the book to Professor Charles Townsend Copeland of Harvard, who urged students to go over and help in any way they could.

The memoir opens at Verdun, in deserted, snow-swept streets, where thoughts of a friendly Harvard hearth seem far away. Later passages explain fortification theory, angles, salients, and bastions, against the concrete walls, bomb-proof shelters, and machine-gun forts of the rear lines. Sheahan writes as an American volunteer among French soldiers, not as a strategist. The book gives a ground-level view of Verdun endurance and of idealism meeting industrial war.
12514-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's fourth volume, Edinburgh and London 1824, continues a general history and collection of voyages and travels arranged in systematic order. The work aims to trace navigation, discovery and commerce by sea and land, from the earliest ages to the present time, illustrated by maps and charts.

Kerr notes that a year had passed since the first half volume, and that its favourable reception encouraged him to continue. Four volumes now stood published, with extensive original accounts among them. This volume carries the survey forward, gathering travellers' reports into one ordered history for readers who wanted the world, explored, in a single shelf.
12960-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for June 1875, volume fifteen number ninety, mixes travel, fiction, poetry, and science for popular readers. Contents include Up the Parana and in Paraguay, a tale of the conscription, and Sidney Lanier's Symphony. Eight hundred miles in an ambulance, a meeting at sea, and William Black's Three Feathers follow, with camp-fire lyrics and Mill's essays on religion.

An ambulance journey passage shows the travel writing. Sandhills track for a thousand miles, a halt comes at Niobrara Creek, pink clover proves bitter weed, and a whirlwind arrives punctually at dinner time. The issue gives a full, varied monthly of 1875. It suits readers of Victorian magazines.
13055-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Volume nine of Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels, dated 1824, carries the English voyages to India after the East India Company took hold. Captain John Saris sails in 1611, notes the Moluccas, reaches Japan, and journeys to the emperor's court, with long accounts of Japanese habits and manners at Firando.

Later logs follow Captain Thomas Elkington from Surat to Bantam in 1615, chasing a Portuguese fleet, sighting water-spouts, and doubling Cape Comorin. The volume shows Kerr's method at full stretch, arranging old ships' journals into a systematic history of navigation and trade.
13061-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for March 1875, volume fifteen, number eighty-seven, mixes fiction, travel, and science for a popular audience. Its contents lead with an escape from Siberia, Australian scenes, a tale of American society, and a paper on Munich as a pest-city. Serial fiction runs beside poems, essays, and notes on the world.

One passage describes a harsh climate where nervous fever is feared most, and sudden winds break the few pleasant days. Another climbs the Sierras, resting on chasm edges where forests and streams lie in shadow far below. The number shows a Victorian monthly at work: varied, illustrated, and eager to carry readers from Siberia to Australia in one sitting.
13116-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for January 1876, volume seventeen, number ninety-seven, opens with The Century: Its Fruits and Its Festival, on general progress. Other contents include Up the Thames by Edward C. Bruce, lines written at Venice by Frances Anne Kemble, sketches of India, and The House on the Beach by Rebecca Harding Davis. Serial fiction and verse fill the rest.

An India sketch takes the reader by rail from Bombay through Salsette to Khandalla, to see the great cave temple of Karli, the largest of its kind in India. Another piece mocks a rector who counts skepticism worse than sepsis, differing by one letter. The number is a solid Victorian monthly, wide in range and sure of its readers.
13130-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels, volume ten, published in 1824, forms a systematic history of navigation, discovery, and commerce by sea and land. This volume continues part two, book four, with early circumnavigations of the world. Its first chapter gives Magellan's voyage of 1519 to 1522, from Seville to Patagonia and on to his death.

Later sections follow fleets to St. Helena, where crews took fish, wood, and water but found goats and oranges hard to get. A Dutch fleet under Heemskirk, fresh from fighting Spaniards near Sal, crosses their path. Another passage tells of thirty men staying with Dampier in the South Sea, while thirty-three sail on. Kerr's collection is a vast, orderly storehouse of travel.
13145-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for April 1873, volume eleven, number twenty-five, leads with Wilmington and its industries, then the Roumi in Kabylia, a Chinese story, and Berrytown by Rebecca Harding Davis. Other contents include The Glaciers of Paradise, Thackeray's Gray Friars by an old gown-boy, and A Princess of Thule by William Black. Monthly gossip closes the issue.

In Thule, Sheila sings in a chapter called Romance-Time, while Berrytown follows Catharine and Kitty through a dinner thick with beef and cabbage. A medical piece weighs expert evidence in poisoning trials, citing Dr. Schoeppe and Mrs. Wharton's Baltimore case. The number is a busy, varied monthly, mixing industry, travel, fiction, and law.
13154-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for February 1876, volume seventeen, number ninety-eight, continues The Century: Its Fruits and Its Festival with American progress. Contents include Up the Thames, concluding paper, by Edward C. Bruce, The Poet's Pen, sketches of India by Emma Lazarus, and The Atonement of Leam Dundas by Mrs. E. Lynn Linton. Letters from South Africa and monthly gossip close the number.

An India sketch breathes cool air among marble whites and green seams, then watches Hindus launch a body into the Nerbudda with calm freedom from grief. A novel passage shows Edgar praising a beautiful face while his mother listens with crisp displeasure and Adelaide pales. The number balances travel, fiction, and centennial pride in one monthly bundle.
13195-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for June 1873, volume eleven, number twenty-seven, offers a full monthly table. It holds A New Atlantis, a paper on the Roumi in Kabylia, a reminiscence of the 1867 Exposition, and Slains Castle by Lady Blanche Murphy. Serials include Our Home in the Tyrol, Saint Romualdo by Emma Lazarus, and A Princess of Thule by William Black. Short pieces and monthly gossip close the number.

Slains Castle's rocks and caves, once a smuggling rendezvous, were made famous by Scott in Guy Mannering. A lugger called the Crooked Mary ran the coast, its skipper's signal halting all ordinary business as folk stole from house to house. The number shows Lippincott's range: travel, fiction, poetry, and talk, all in one popular monthly.
13225-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages, volume six, published in 1824, continues part two, book two, with early English voyages to America. Sections cover the Cabots' discovery of Newfoundland in 1497 for Henry VII, discourses on Cabot, and later voyages north and west. Kerr arranges his material in systematic order, from earliest ages to his own time.

One passage follows Albuquerque to a palace ringed by armed men, where Coutinno waits in danger and sends word to follow after gathering his men. Another describes a harbor safe in all weathers, eight or nine fathoms deep, entered from the northeast between island and mainland. The volume is a solid, source-based record of early Atlantic exploration.
13242-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for April 1876, volume seventeen, number one hundred, carries The Century series to the Centennial Exposition under roof. Contents include the conclusion of Sketches of India, The College Student by James Morgan Hart, The House That Susan Built, and The Berkshire Lady by Thomas Hughes. Leam Dundas's atonement continues through chapters on Maya and delusion.

A college essay argues that the best education is more than perfect recitations and keeping out of mischief, since small colleges would otherwise win by default. A novel passage shows Leam, grave and serious-eyed, failing to charm a child who dreams in terror after too much cake. The number marks a magazine at its hundredth issue, confident and varied.
13287-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages, volume seven, published in 1824, continues part two, book three, with Portuguese Asia and voyages in Egypt, Syria, and Arabia. Sections cover a Portuguese expedition from India to Madagascar in 1613, and Portuguese dealings in India from 1617 to 1640. Kerr's order is systematic, from earliest ages to his own time.

One passage shows a governor taking a traveler aside to learn what Calicut's king planned against Christians, then sending him by galley under Joam Serano to the viceroy at Cochin. Another lists ships of a 1566 Plymouth fleet, the Castle of Comfort, the May-Flower, and the George, sailing past Ushant and Finisterre. The volume is a dense, source-rich history of sea power.
13366-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels, volume eight, Edinburgh 1824, continues early English voyages to the East Indies before an exclusive company existed. Contents cover John Eldred's voyage by sea to Tripoli in Syria and by land to Bagdat and Basora in 1583. They add monsoons by William Barret, and the first English voyage to India in 1591 under Captain George Raymond. Kerr arranges voyages in systematic order.

Merchants at Acheen wait for pepper, which comes slowly after a sterile year, then send the Susan to Priaman in Sumatra under Henry Middleton. The general grieves that chief pilot John Davis promised pepper at four Spanish ryals of eight the hundred, while it cost almost twice that. Later, travelers pass Broach, a fair castle on the Nerbuddah, and buy fine baffatas surpassing Holland cloth. The volume is a rich source for early trade.
13381-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels, volume fourteen, Edinburgh and London 1824, gives James Cook's account of a voyage towards the South Pole. Cook sailed round the world in the Resolution and Adventure, 1772 to 1775. Contents run from Dusky Bay to Queen Charlotte's Sound, water spouts, and Captain Furneaux's narrative after the ships parted. Kerr's collection arranges voyages in systematic order.

At Dusky Bay, Forster speaks in poetical feeling of fair weather, lightly wafting airs, evergreens mingling with autumn yellow, and wild notes of birds, moving the whole crew to emotion. Later, Cook describes low coral isles ranged in a circle, joined by a reef, their inland seas full of fish and turtle, excellent harbors shut up from shipping. The volume is a major source for Pacific exploration.
13440-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for January 1875, volume fifteen, mixes travel, fiction, and science for a popular audience. The New Hyperion carries readers from Paris to Marly by way of the Rhine, Following the Tiber offers two papers on Rome. Malcolm runs through chapters on a laird, his mother, and a cry from the chamber.

Poems by Charlotte F. Bates and F. A. Hillard, Edward C. Bruce's Leaden Arrow, and William Black's Three Feathers, with Tintagel's walls and a confession, fill the literary pages. R. Davey's Stage in Italy describes the diurno, an open-air amphitheatre theatre with tiered seats and a covered corridor. The number is a full Victorian monthly in miniature.
13606-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Volume eighteen of Robert Kerr's vast history of voyages and travels, printed at Edinburgh in 1824. Carries William Stevenson's historical sketch of discovery, navigation, and commerce from the earliest records to the start of the nineteenth century. Maps and charts support a systematic account of how seafaring grew into world trade.

Stevenson traces Roman and British ventures, including Caesar's invasions of Britain with hundreds of ships, and follows the rise of Dutch, Spanish, and French commerce. He weighs why wealth flowed to some nations and not others, tying trade to ships, colonies, and coin. The volume works as a survey of exploration before steam, written when Britain's sea power stood at its height.
13636-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for February 1873, volume eleven, opens with a concluding paper searching for the quinine plant in Peru. A glance at the site and antiquities of Athens by J. L. T. Phillips, Constance Fenimore Woolson's Commonplace, and Caroline Chesebro's Probationer Leonhard follow, with country-house life in England and the Forest of Arden.

A diver's tale of monitors, small square hatches, and a swinging ladder down into recesses shows the issue's taste for adventure. Young eyes saddened by a painful problem are promised morning mists breaking and a conquering sun enfolding humble laurels and great pines alike. The magazine mixes travel, fiction, and science for a general readership.
13655-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for March 1876 gathers fiction, travel writing, and general essays in one monthly issue. It opens with a survey of past expositions and the century's festivals. Sketches of India and letters from South Africa follow, alongside notes on life-saving stations by Rebecca Harding Davis. A serial novel by Mrs. E. Lynn Linton runs through the middle.

The mix shows what a middle-class American magazine offered its readers. Science, art, and foreign life sit beside domestic fiction and poetry. Short pieces keep the pace brisk, while longer articles dig into one topic at a time. The issue also records Victorian views of empire, industry, and progress. It works as both light reading and a window on 1870s taste.
13770-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for December 1873 mixes serial fiction with travel, history, and science. A new Hyperion story and a Princess of Thule serial anchor the fiction. Sketches of Eastern travel take readers to Bangkok, while other pieces visit the national capital and Florida sport. Poems and short essays fill the remaining pages.

The issue shows a popular magazine balancing entertainment and instruction. Illustrations support the travel writing and add colour to the fiction. William Black's serial, then in mid-course, follows Scottish life and romance. Shorter items touch Monaco, science, and current affairs. Together they capture American magazine taste in the early 1870s.
13828-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for August 1873 offers fiction, travel, and science in monthly form. The New Hyperion continues, alongside Our Home in the Tyrol by Margaret Howitt. Inside Japan by W. E. Griffis and Jason's Quest by Charles Warren Stoddard add foreign colour. William Black's Princess of Thule reaches its transformation chapters.

Short pieces on church steps, deer parks, and tropical fruits round out the number. Fannie R. Feudge rambles among fruits and flowers of the tropics in two papers. The mix of serial, sketch, and essay suited a broad middle-class audience. Illustrations support the travel writing. The issue captures American magazine life in the Gilded Age.
13956-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for May 1876 continues its blend of exhibition news, travel, and serial fiction. The Century's fruits and festival, minor structures of the exhibition, opens with illustrations. Glimpses of Constantinople by Sheila Hale and Berlin and Vienna by James Morgan Hart follow. Margaret J. Preston's Ballad of the Bell-Tower adds verse.

Mrs. E. Lynn Linton's Atonement of Leam Dundas reaches chapters on marriage, love, Dunaston Castle, and letters of fire. Sidney Lanier's Rose-Morals and a note on kindergartens close the variety. The kindergarten, the writer notes, trains a child's body as thoroughly as mind. The issue captures Centennial-year magazine culture.
13964-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for October 1873 mixes travel, fiction, and poetry. Edward Strahan takes readers from Paris to Marly by way of the Rhine, with a day in Strasburg. A piece from the Potomac to the Ohio and a strong-minded woman's episode add American colour. The King of Bavaria and a strange land and peculiar people follow.

Sarah C. Hallowell's On the Church Steps continues, with Margaret Howitt's Tyrol home. William Black's Princess of Thule advances through exchanges and guesses. A shell falls on the Bank of France during bombardment, shattering stairs within. The issue balances war news with domestic serials. It captures magazine variety in the 1870s.
14036-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for September 1873 offers serials, travel, and verse. Edward Strahan's New Hyperion reaches the Feast of Saint Athanasius. Martin I. Griffin tells the Ride of Prince Geraint, while William Black's Princess of Thule deepens. Sketches of Eastern travel visit the Count de Beauvoir in China.

Margaret Howitt's Tyrol home continues, with Fannie R. Feudge concluding tropical fruits and flowers. A lotos of the Nile and an echo poem add verse. A confused narrator forgets an engagement with Grandstone, living now, the engineer reminds him. The issue balances adventure with domestic serials. It captures 1870s magazine reading.
14324-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for April 1875 mixes travel, fiction, and science for a general reader. Australian scenes close a long series, and William Black's Three Feathers runs on through new chapters. A piece on the golden eagle and his eyrie joins a sonnet and a sketch of Nice. The Raskol, a study of Russian sects, opens a longer inquiry. Emma Lazarus adds a short poem, A March Violet.

Nice comes alive in a sketch of Madame Rattazzi, who promenades in purple velvet edged with canary satin. She spends five months each winter in Nice, each day in a fresh dress, and lights her windows in Italian colors to spite a dowager below. A second piece asks what a conclave is, and traces how popes came to be chosen by cardinals alone. The number pairs society gossip with church history, and travel with fiction.
14327-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for January 1873 mixes fact pieces, tales, and verse for a general reader. Edward Rowland writes on iron bridges and how they are built. Another piece tracks the hunt for the quinine plant in Peru. Caroline Chesebro' adds a serial tale, Probationer Leonhard, set in a place called the Happy Valley. Poems, travel notes, and short fiction fill out the number.

Longer pieces look at Ireland's capital and at old scandals of high life. One tells of Lady Belvedere, shut up for eighteen years in a gloomy house after a trial for adultery. A second gives a traveler's memories of Florence, stitched from chance meetings and old names. A third turns on a ghostly figure at sea and a sapphire that links two lives. The mix shows what a popular monthly offered its readers in 1873: news of science, art, and far places, beside romance and gossip.
14333-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for June 1876 mixes a centennial survey with fiction and travel. A long piece on the Century's fruits and festival opens the number. Emma Lazarus adds Dolores, and Sheila Hale closes her glimpses of Constantinople. Edward Kearsley writes Thee and You, a story of old Philadelphia. James M. Bruce tells of modern Huguenots in the Alps. The number shows a monthly at full stretch.

The Huguenot piece follows Felix Neff, sent to Dauphiné as a young minister in 1824. His flock, long denied citizenship and treated as outcasts, kept a stubborn force of character. A second thread, Felipa by Constance Fenimore Woolson, turns on a girl whose trouble her kin read as love nonsense. Her brother calls the man a fool and a coward, and hopes fell air will brisk her up. The number pairs history with romance, and faith with feeling.
14423-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's vast collection of voyages reaches its twelfth volume with the Pacific voyages ordered by George III, published in Edinburgh in 1824. The volume opens with Commodore Byron's circumnavigation in the Dolphin.

It continues with Wallis, Carteret, and the early voyages of James Cook, recording latitudes, winds, birds, and landfalls day by day. Maps and charts accompanied the original edition. Kerr's compilation gathers official journals into one systematic history of navigation, discovery, and commerce, and it remains a rich source on eighteenth-century exploration. Later volumes carry the story to other oceans and centuries.
14464-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's thirteenth volume of voyages, published in 1824, continues Cook's Pacific journals with detailed descriptions of Tahiti and New Zealand. The systematic collection aimed to cover navigation from the earliest ages to its own day.

Sections describe Tahitian produce, dress, houses, food, boats, language, religion, war, and government, then move to New Zealand coasts, Poor Knights Islands, and native houses glimpsed from shipboard. Kerr's text preserves the explorers' daily reckonings of wind and latitude. The volume is a key source on first European contacts in the South Pacific. Kerr's notes on Tahitian customs remain widely cited by historians.
14611-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's fifteenth volume of voyages continues James Cook's second voyage toward the South Pole and round the world, in the Resolution and Adventure during 1772 to 1775. Blackwood and Cadell published the collection in 1824.

The volume follows Cook from New Zealand round Cape Horn, through the Strait of Le Maire, and home to England, with reflections on island peoples and their new ideas from European contact. Kerr's compilation preserves Cook's journals in systematic order. It remains a key source on Pacific exploration in the age of sail. Kerr's systematic order made Cook's journals easy to consult.
14691-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for July 1873, volume twelve, number twenty-eight, mixes fiction, travel, and science for Philadelphia readers. Edward Strahan's New Hyperion leads the contents.

Other items include a journey from Philadelphia to Baltimore, Rebecca Harding Davis's Berrytown, strange sea industries, a Tyrol home, the American ambulance corps at Paris, and notes on Shelley's early history. A traveler among palmetto channels hears a distant cry mistaken for waterfowl. The issue shows a general magazine serving many tastes in one cover. Lippincott's Philadelphia monthly ran fiction, travel, and science side by side for decades.
14709-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for February 1875 gathers fiction, travel and science in one thick monthly number. Following the Tiber concludes, and Six Months Among Cannibals reports from afar. An American girl and her lovers, a Japanese marriage in high life and a lost baby supply the domestic and foreign tales.

William Black's Three Feathers runs through its later chapters, while Sidney Lanier writes on corn, H. C. Wood on fever, and T. Adolphus Trollope recalls the sculptor Hiram Powers. Sonnets, a singular family and Gentleman Dick round out the mix. The issue shows a Victorian magazine at work: entertainment, instruction and curiosity bound together for a general reader.
14842-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine for September 1880 opens with a cross-country trip across Florida lakes to Ekoniah Scrub. A county clerk folds his map and tells the travellers to find William Townsend if they get lost. The strange amphibious land goes on turning solid ground into marshy prairies and prairies into lakes.

Bright, sparkling sapphires threaded through the landscape give the piece its colour. Around it, the monthly number keeps Lippincott's usual blend of fiction, travel and science for general readers. The Florida sketch is the heart of this issue: a tour of a half-water country, told by people who crossed it by lake and scrub rather than by rail.
14984-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
A general history and collection of voyages and travels, in a volume devoted largely to Peru and Chile, traces Spanish conquest and colonial trouble in South America. Gonzalo Pizarro's usurpation, Pedro de la Gasca's expedition and the death of Gonzalo, and insurrection in Nicaragua open the sequence.

Peru under viceroys from Antonio de Mendoza to the Marquis del Cannete follows, with incidents under successive governments. Chile's origin, manners and language, Spanish expeditions under Almagro and Pedro de Valdivia, and the long war with Araucanians complete the picture. The collection is a standard early source for South American colonial history, gathered from many voyages.
15376-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's General History and Collection of Voyages and Travels, volume eleven, printed at Edinburgh and London in 1824, gathers sea and land journeys from earliest ages to his present time. Maps and charts illustrate the set, arranged in systematic order to trace navigation, discovery, and commerce. Part two, book four, continues here.

Captain George Shelvocke's voyage round the world in 1719 to 1722 features, with a passage from California to Canton. Kerr's collection served readers who wanted the world's voyages in one place. Travel historians will find the volume a rich, if dated, treasury of exploration.
15425-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr compiled this seventeenth volume of his great history of voyages and travels, printed in Edinburgh in 1824. The series arranges accounts of navigation, discovery, and trade by sea and land, from the earliest ages to Kerr's own day, in systematic order. Maps and charts illustrate the text.

This volume continues Captain King's journal of the return to the Sandwich Islands, now Hawaii, after Captain Cook's death. Long sections describe each island: its coasts, volcanoes, snowy peaks, climate, winds, animals, and plants. Later parts turn to the islanders themselves, their customs, crafts, and rule. It preserves an early European record of Hawaii, valuable for its detail even where its judgments now read as dated.
16011-the-emigrants-of-ahadarra-the-work:
William Carleton opens this Irish novel on a summer morning. A small man dressed as a beggar walks with a slender girl of about sixteen. They head toward the house of a well-off farmer. The house stands on a rise above the highway, long and slated, with an air of plenty mixed with slovenly neglect. The scene sets Carleton's familiar ground: Irish farm folk, their homes, and their habits.

The title points to the larger theme, as families weigh leaving Ahadarra for a new life across the sea. Carleton follows their hopes, quarrels, and partings with sympathy and homely humor. The book gives modern readers a vivid picture of rural Ireland at a time when emigration was reshaping whole parishes.
16471-a-general-history-and-collection-o:
Robert Kerr's sixteenth volume of voyages and travels, printed in Edinburgh in 1824, follows Captain Cook's later voyage to Otaheite and the Society Islands, then toward the coast of North America. An eclipse of the moon, the discovery of Toobouai, and Omai's reception open the account, with interviews with island chiefs and notes on dress, canoes, and customs.

Kerr arranged his vast collection in systematic order, forming a complete history of navigation and discovery. Maps and charts illustrate the text. Readers of voyage literature will find this volume a rich slice of Pacific exploration, told with eighteenth-century detail and curiosity.
19032-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
This July 1878 issue of Lippincott's Magazine mixes popular literature and science for general readers. It opens in old Bristol, with narrow streets, gabled houses, charity children in old dress, and the grave of Hannah More. The city's literary past runs through the piece.

Later pages visit a Gothic cathedral, with tombs of Bishop Butler, Mrs. Draper, and Lady Hesketh, and a bust of Southey in his native town. Stories, verse, and science notes fill the rest. Readers get a Victorian magazine miscellany, learned, chatty, and keen on place and history.
19093-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
The October 1878 number of Lippincott's Magazine opens in Warwick and Coventry. There English history lives in provincial towns. Old noble houses now mask hotels, schools, and clubs. Cottages, balconies, and oriels suggest romance and antique charm. Modern life sits uneasily on old stones.

Later pieces wander spring gardens full of crocuses and daffodils. They meet a clever clergyman storyteller. He keeps a notebook so he never repeats an anecdote. Stories, verse, and science notes complete the number. Readers get a rich Victorian miscellany on town, country, and letters, full of colour and charm. The whole number feels warm and varied.
20583-the-tribes-and-castes-of-the-centr:
The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces of India is a large official survey of the peoples of central India. Compiled under British rule, it describes tribe by tribe, caste by caste, their customs, gods, work, and kinship rules. Each group gets its own careful entry.

A note singles out the Gonds as the most important of the non-Aryan or primitive tribes, whose social customs are described in detail. The Baiga, Bhil, Kawar, Khond, Kol, Korku, and Korwa stand among the other major tribes covered. Whatever its colonial frame, the survey preserves a vast record of Indian social life.
20668-the-tribes-and-castes-of-the-centr:
This volume of The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces of India continues the great ethnographic survey of the region. Entries describe each tribe and caste: its legends, marriages, funerals, gods, and work. The volume opens with help for readers facing Indian words in English letters.

Its pronunciation key explains that one a has the sound of u in but or murmur. Another a sounds as in bath or tar. The letter e matches the sound in the French word écarté, and i may sound as in bit. With that key, readers could speak the names of the Gonds, Bhils, and hundreds of smaller groups the survey records.
22010-the-tribes-and-castes-of-the-centr:
R. V. Russell of the Indian Civil Service directed the ethnographic survey of India's Central Provinces. Working with Rai Bahadur Hira Lal, he produced The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces of India in four volumes, printed in 1916. Volume II runs through the alphabet from the Agaria iron-workers onward. Each article treats one caste or tribe in turn.

Entries describe a group's work, customs, marriage rules, gods, and place in village life. Herdsmen, merchants, forest tribes, robbers turned labourers, and holy beggars all appear. The book was an official record, made so district officers could know the people they governed. Today it stands as a vast, flawed snapshot of Indian society under British rule.
22172-the-knickerbocker-or-new-york-mont:
The Knickerbocker was New York's leading literary monthly in the 1840s. This number, volume 23 for May 1844, opens with Thomas Carlyle on Napoleon Bonaparte. The editors compiled the piece from Carlyle's works, offering all he had published on Napoleon in one place. It stands in for a fuller article they could not get.

Around it sit poems, tales, reviews, and the editor's table talk that made the magazine famous. The Knickerbocker published Irving's circle and set New York's literary tone for a generation. A single issue preserves that tone: ambitious, clubbable, and proud of American letters. It also shows how American magazines fed readers on British lions like Carlyle.
22402-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science mixed essays, fiction, and bold ideas. One passage dreams of a cloud observed hanging over Washington. The writer would annex it by electrical communications in every direction.

A resident governor would sit fixed at the cloud's center in a balloon. The same pages turn to France and Algeria with equal confidence. France has gorged Kabylia, the writer says, but never digested it. Such leaps show the magazine's free-ranging nineteenth-century mind. Science, empire, and fancy shared its pages without apology. Readers get a period monthly in full flight, part journal and part speculation.
23095-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Kabylia opens this volume of Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science. The inhabitants of Kalaa pass for rich, a traveler writes. Kalaa's women walk unveiled and jeweled, its streets unusually clean for Kabylia. Four sheikhs govern the place, and the travelers carry an introduction to one of them.

Their safe-conduct, the anaya, holds good. An imposing elder in a white burnoose receives the party with warmth under a stately manner. Travel, fiction, poetry, and science share Lippincott's pages in the Philadelphia monthly's usual blend. A bound volume like this one was a middle-class library in itself. Its Algerian journey shows the reach of its curiosity, and its confidence.
26276-history-of-company-e-of-the-sixth-:
Alfred J. Hill's 1899 history of Company E, Sixth Minnesota Regiment of Volunteer Infantry, with an appendix by Captain Charles J. Stees, began as a home-made record. Its preface faults subscription company histories sold in camps as mere broadsides from muster rolls. Hill's own work started while the regiment lay at New Orleans, and it was kept up in the field until the order home.

Serious illness and the scattering of the men delayed its finish for years. Mid-book marches cross Minnesota country, reach a camp of friendly Indians, and free white captives at a place later called Camp Release, near the Chippewa and Minnesota rivers. The book serves as a plain, first-hand record of one company's war service.
2871-the-variation-of-animals-and-plants:
Charles Darwin's Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication, first volume, opens his full case for how domestic breeding reshapes species. Darwin catalogs pigeon breeds in fine detail, noting one breed larger than the rock pigeon, with a smaller beak, smaller feet, a forehead spot, and a white body. He dates the breed to 1676 through Willughby's Ornithology and notes that it still bred true in his own day.

The volume builds toward the argument that human selection, working over generations, can produce the same kinds of change as nature. Darwin piles up examples from birds, animals, and plants before drawing conclusions. Readers who know only the Origin will find here the workshop evidence behind its theory.
2872-the-variation-of-animals-and-plants:
Charles Darwin's Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication, second volume, gathers the evidence for how breeding changes living things. Darwin studies pigeons, flowers, and farm stock, asking how selection by breeders produces new forms from old ones. A passage on double flowers notes stunted wild gentian plants on a poor chalky bank, and cites garden writers on the same effect.

The volume supports the argument of On the Origin of Species with masses of observed detail, from bud variation to the inheritance of habits. Darwin weighs rival explanations carefully and admits where evidence runs thin. It remains a key work for readers who want Darwin's reasoning at full length rather than in summary.
28897-the-variation-of-animals-and-plant:
Charles Darwin wrote this second volume of The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication, published by John Murray in London in 1868. Its chapters treat inheritance in all its forms: pedigrees of domestic animals, trifling characters inherited, diseases inherited, longevity and vigor, and extra digits regrowing after amputation. A following chapter treats reversion, or atavism, in pigeons, fowls, cattle, sheep, and cultivated plants.

Darwin gathers cases from breeders, doctors, and his own reading to ask how much of a creature comes from its parents and how much from its life. The volume stands as the groundwork for his later theory of pangenesis. Readers get Darwin the collector at his fullest, patient, curious, and willing to follow a small fact wherever it leads.
29184-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
J. B. Lippincott and Company published this May 1875 number of Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science. Its opening travel piece, Up the Parana and in Paraguay, begins with the foreigner's lot in Buenos Aires during the rainy season. Houses built against summer heat let winter damp through doors and windows, and endless rain drives Englishmen to spleen and Americans to the blues.

The issue also carries fiction, including a serial reaching chapter thirty-three, with chapters titled Three Feathers, Some Old Friends, and A Dark Conspiracy. Readers get a month of a popular Victorian magazine, mixing South American travel with serial romance and intrigue for a general audience.
31365-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Volume twenty-six of Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science, published in Philadelphia in 1880, offers a full half-year of American magazine reading. Serial fiction runs through its pages, including Adam and Eve by the author of Dorothy Fox and the novels Nan, Jack, Diet and its Doings, and Jan of the North. Stories, poems, and illustrated travel pieces fill the rest.

Nonfiction ranges from American exploration and aeronauts to a Rocky-Mountain outpost, Dungeness plantation, Florida lakes, canoeing on the high Mississippi, Portugal, Limoges porcelain, horse-racing in France, and automatism by Dr. H. C. Wood. With contributions from William H. Rideing, Charles Burr Todd, Henry A. Beers, Lucy H. Hooper, and many others, the volume captures Gilded Age popular letters at their most varied.
31750-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science, volume twenty, was published at Philadelphia by J. B. Lippincott and Company in 1877, entered the same year. Its contents run from H. James Jr.'s Abbeys and Castles and David Ker's Day's March through Finland to E. C. Hewitt's Few Letters and a great day from the Italian of Edmondo de Amicis. A Kentucky Duel by Will Wallace Harney and Rebecca Harding Davis's Law unto Herself also appear.

The volume mixes travel, fiction, and comment, as a monthly magazine of popular literature and science should. Its pages show the magazine's range, from European castles to American duels, in a single bound volume of 1877.
31946-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science, September 1877, opens among the Kabyles, with remnants of old peoples tucked into odd corners all over the earth. Its first paper describes a people driven by foreign invasion from the plains into the rocks, markedly different from specimens preserved elsewhere.

Later pages of the issue turn to American fiction, including a chapter in which Judge Rhodes, breakfasting in New York with the editor Mr. Neckart, finds him grown lean and sallow, secretive and irritable, holding himself in under constant self-control. Readers get a full Victorian magazine issue, mixing travel, science, and serialized story.
33550-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This volume of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica covers entries from Bisharin to Bohea, in alphabetical order. Its articles span peoples, places, history, and science, each set out in the dense, exact style of the great reference work. Readers will find long treatments of major topics beside short entries on smaller terms, all arranged for quick lookup.

As a slice of the famous eleventh edition, the volume shows how knowledge was summed up before the First World War: thorough, confident, and rich in detail. It serves best as a work to dip into, whether for a tribe, a town, or a term in science. Scholars still prize this edition, and this volume gives a full taste of its scope.
33558-thoracic-and-coracoid-arteries-in-:
Marion Anne Jenkinson compares the chest and shoulder arteries of two bird families, the pigeons and doves and the swallows. Working from specimens held at the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History, she dissected birds preserved in alcohol and examined their blood vessels under a binocular microscope. The study covers four kinds of pigeon and dove and five kinds of swallow.

Its sections describe the muscles and vessels of each family in turn, then summarize how the arterial pattern is arranged and where it varies. Jenkinson notes differences within families and between them, and discusses what that variation may mean. Seven figures support the descriptions, making the paper a detailed anatomical reference for students of bird structure.
34578-the-life-or-legend-of-gaudama-the-:
Bigandet sets down a faith's founder in The Life or Legend of Gaudama, the Buddha of the Burmese, volume 1, printed in London in 1911. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner made the book, in the Oriental Series, here in a fourth edition of two volumes. Annotations attend the text, with the ways to Neibban and a notice on the Phongyies, or Burmese monks.

Bigandet was bishop of Ramatha and vicar apostolic of Ava and Pegu. Parts of the work first appeared in a journal of the Indian Archipelago, from 1852 to 1855. A first complete edition was printed at Rangoon in 1858, and a second, much enlarged, in 1866. Very few copies of either reached Europe, a note says, and both are entirely out of print.
37122-hunting-in-many-lands-the-book-of-:
Hunting in Many Lands is the 1895 book of the Boone and Crockett Club, edited by Theodore Roosevelt and George Bird Grinnell. The Forest and Stream Publishing Company issued it in New York. Club members report big-game hunts on four continents, and the volume also carries the club's constitution, officers, and member list.

Contents run from W A Chanler in East Africa and a moose hunt by Madison Grant to Elliott Roosevelt in India and wolf-hunting in Russia. A bear hunt in the Sierras and Theodore Roosevelt in the cattle country follow. Later chapters turn to game laws and the protection of Yellowstone National Park, with the park acts printed in full. The book records both the sport and the early game-protection cause that the club was founded to advance.
37946-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science, for December 1877, is a monthly book of tales and fact. The lead piece is A Month in Sicily, first paper. Dawn finds its party on a steamer for Palermo on the first of February, sun up over the sea.

Land in the south turns from blue to brown and red peaks, with orange farms at their feet. The writer calls Sicily a land all who love verse, romance, or old life must long to see. Greek tales set giants, the Cyclops, and the nymph Arethusa there. Greek colons made Naxos in 735 years prior to Christ, by the slopes of Etna. More of the isle was Greek in three hundred years. Travel fans get a rich first look at a famed isle.
38401-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume XII, Slice VII of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Gyantse to Hallel. The slice opens with a full list of its articles, set out in two columns. Names and topics range from Gyges and gymnastics to habeas corpus and Hakluyt.

Readers find short entries on places such as Gyantse, Gyula-Fehérvár, and Haarlem set beside longer pieces on science and law. The gyroscope and gyrostat article is a long technical piece. Gynaecology, gypsum, and gymnosperms sit near lives of writers, soldiers, and church figures. The whole slice shows how the set mixed geography, biography, science, and history in strict letter order.
39180-ti-ping-tien-kwoh-the-history-of-t:
Ti Ping Tien Kwoh is a history of the Ti Ping revolution in China. Lin Le, a former officer of the Chung Wang guards, wrote the account. Day and Son of London issued the two part work in eighteen sixty six. Lin Le also led the Loyal and Faithful Auxiliary Legion in the war.

A commission from Le, the Faithful Prince, fronts the book in Chinese script. That paper certifies Lin Le work between Shanghai and Ningpo in war service. He managed war affairs and ships and gathered stores on those runs. The history joins that personal record with a narrative of his adventures. Readers get an inside view of the Ti Ping cause from a foreign officer.
39423-the-manual-of-the-botany-of-the-no:
Asa Gray made this guide to the plants of the north of the United States. The sixth shape of the book came out in 1890, made fresh and spread west to the line of the 100th degree. Sereno Watson and John M. Coulter did that work, with the aid of men skilled in set groups. Gray had been Fisher Professor of Natural History at Harvard. Watson kept the Gray Herbarium at the same school.

The range of the book is the district east of the Mississippi and north of North Carolina and Tennessee. It holds twenty-five plates, which show the sedges, the grass kind, and the ferns. The list of parts shows its tools: a brief of the orders, a key that works by choice of marks, and lists of short forms and signs.
39632-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, the slice running from Harmony to Heanor, is one part of the great reference work of 1910 and 1911. This text of it was made by volunteer proofreaders. Their notes explain the marks used for subscripts and roots, and list the misprints they corrected as they went. The slice is alphabetical, article by article, in the manner of the whole work.

The notes name the articles they touched. Harmony, the music article, speaks of the key feeling shared by major and minor, and of Haydn and Mozart borrowing across the modes. Harmotome, a mineral, is placed at Andreasberg in the Harz. Lives follow: Ernest Abraham Hart, the sanitary reformer, and Sir Robert Hart of the China consular service. William Harvey, found cheerful and sprightly in study, and the Indian town of Hathras stand further along the alphabet.
39845-early-illustrated-books-a-history-:
Alfred Pollard wrote a history of the decoration and illustration of books in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, first issued in 1893 and revised for a second edition in 1917. It belongs to a series of books about books that Pollard himself edited. The first chapter treats the rubricators and illuminators who finished early printed books by hand.

Chapters then follow the printed picture country by country: Germany in two, Italy in two, France with its books of hours, Holland, and Spain. Gordon Duff contributes the chapter on England. Pollard opens by insisting that the first printers had to make the utmost of their new art to justify its right to exist. Collectors and librarians are the audience.
40784-ossian-in-germany-bibliography-gen:
Ossian in Germany is a scholarly study by Rudolf Tombo, sometime fellow in German at Columbia University, copyrighted by Columbia University Press in 1901. AMS Press reprinted it at New York in 1966. It joins a bibliography and general survey to an account of Ossian's influence on Klopstock and the bards.

The preface explains how the work outgrew its plan: material found in the British Museum led to a card index of German Ossianiana. Libraries in Germany then added material so fast that a chronological bibliography suggested itself. That bibliography grew so large that Tombo published it as the introduction to the literary material. The literary discussion is therefore confined to one period, keeping chronological sequence. Material on the Storm and Stress poets, the Göttingen circle, and the Romantic school was collected for later treatment.
4108-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
A volume of Filson Young's Columbus biography begins with the home in Genoa and the hard question of ancestry. How far back should a life go, Young asks, when character passes mysteriously through parents, flesh of their flesh and bone of their bone.

The admiral adds only his own personality to that common stock, yet that addition changed the world. Young builds Columbus from family, city, and sea, before the great voyage enters the tale. Readers who like biography that starts at the roots will enjoy this thoughtful opening volume.
4109-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
Filson Young's life of Columbus follows the admiral on the long road from Santa Fe to Huelva, on foot, with a sad heart and a small talking boy. Each step carries him farther from the glittering scene where his hopes once shone bright and have now fallen to dust.

The chapter, Our Lady of La Rabida, brings Columbus to the friary where his cause found shelter and friends. Young writes with sympathy for the dreamer's pride and weariness. Readers who like narrative biography will find a moving passage on hope deferred, before the voyage that changed the world.
4110-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
Young's life of Columbus follows the admiral after weighing anchor on November 12, with six captive Indians aboard. He seeks the island of Babeque, said to lie thirty leagues east-southeast, where people gathered gold from sand by candlelight at night.

The Indians told him this by signs, and Columbus shaped his course by their report, hammering bars of hope from rumor. Young tells the first voyage as a mix of navigation, wonder, and error. Readers will enjoy a vivid passage on how gold fever steered the ships of discovery. Gold fever steers ships as surely as wind does.
4111-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
In Young's life of Columbus, the busy months of July, August, and September 1493, when Columbus prepared his second voyage. He superintended the buying, building, and fitting of ships, the choice of stores, and the selection of his company.

Fourteen caravels, some of light draught fit for rivers, joined three large carracks of three to four hundred tons. Volunteers flocked to a venture now backed by royal favor. Readers who like the business of exploration will enjoy this detailed account of how a fleet for the New World was made ready.
4112-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
The conquest of Espanola fills this part of Young's Columbus life, after Columbus left the island under his brother James. Ojeda marched into the interior and took command of Fort St. Thomas, freeing Margarite to lead a reconnoitering expedition through the island.

Young follows soldiers, forts, and Native peoples through a hard campaign of control and resistance. The volume shows discovery turning into dominion, with all its violence and confusion. Readers who want the story past the landing will find this a sobering, necessary part of the tale. Discovery has turned into dominion, and the cost is plain.
4113-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
Young's Columbus biography pauses here for an interlude, stepping back from the admiral's perilous balancing act on Espanola. Columbus's true work, Young argues, was already done when he struck the rock of western discovery and springs flowed from it.

Some of those springs would run in mightier channels than his own, as other men stirred by news of the first voyage set out on their own courses. The volume widens the view from one man to a whole age of voyagers. Readers will enjoy a reflective passage on fame, legacy, and the many hands that followed Columbus west.
4114-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
Chains at Cadiz mark the crisis in Young's life of Columbus of the admiral's life, when ships from Villegio reached Cadiz in October bearing Columbus in manacles. The sight of an admiral in chains stirred pity beyond his highest hopes.

Now in his fiftieth year, of venerable aspect, with white hair and beard and a kindling eye under white brows, Columbus faced disgrace and vindication at once. Young weighs the fall of a hero against the envy of rivals. Readers will find this volume the biography's dramatic low point, and its moral center.
4115-christopher-columbus-and-the-new-wo:
The admiral comes home in this late part of Young's Columbus biography for the last time. On September 12, 1504, Columbus completed at San Domingo the simple preparations for his final voyage, his Jamaica ship refitted under his brother Bartholomew, plus a small new caravel.

The man who had so often fitted ships in port now made ready for a crossing he would not repeat. Young writes the closing voyage with gravity, weighing glory against age and disappointment. Readers who have followed Columbus from Genoa will find this volume a sober, fitting farewell to the admiral.
41424-the-tribes-and-castes-of-the-centr:
The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces of India, by Russell of the Indian Civil Service, assisted by Hira Lal, was published in four volumes by Macmillan in 1916. This third volume continues the alphabetical survey of the region's communities, from Gadaria shepherds and Gadba forest tribes onward. The work was issued under the orders of the Central Provinces administration.

Each article describes a caste or tribe: its work, customs, religion, and place in village life. Entries range from weavers, herdsmen, and grass-cutters to astrologers, liquor vendors, and village watchmen. Compiled for administrators, the survey is now read as a vast, if dated, record of central Indian society at the close of the British period.
41771-the-history-of-sulu:
The History of Sulu, by Najeeb Saleeby, forms part two of volume four of the Ethnological Survey Publications, printed at Manila by the Bureau of Public Printing in 1908.

Its chapters first describe the Sulu Archipelago geographically, island by island, with the town of Jolo, its trade, and its population. A genealogy follows, with the translator's introduction, the descendants of Asip and of Tuan Masha'ika, and the original and later settlers. The history proper runs from Sulu before Islam through the rise of a Mohammedan dynasty under Abu Bakr and the early sultanate. Later chapters treat Figueroa's expeditions, Moro raids, the first Spanish conquest, the treaty of 1836 printed in full, and the cession of the Borneo possessions in 1878.
42552-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Slice seven of volume seventeen of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, runs from Mars to Matteawan. The set bills itself as a dictionary of arts, sciences, literature, and general information. A list at the front gives every article in the slice. Mars, Marsala, and Marseilles stand near the start. Marsh and Marshall entries follow in a long run.

Biographies include Alfred Marshall, John Marshall the jurist, and Andrew Marvell. Karl Marx gets an article, as does Mary Queen of Scots. Place articles cover towns, islands, and regions across the world. Notes at the front record small fixes made in copying the text. The slice shows the range of the great edition in one short stretch of the alphabet.
42854-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The volume of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, kept here runs by its title from Magnetite to Malt. What the opening pages give is the transcriber's list of fixes made while typing the text. That list is itself a map of the volume's goods, naming article after article in order.

Magnetometer and Magneto-Optics come early, with Heinrich Gustav Magnus and his green salt among the lives. Mahomet and Mahommedan Law follow, then the Malay Archipelago, the Malays, and the Malay States, with Bantam renamed Batavia along the way. Science, faith, and empire thus share one stretch of the alphabet, as they do throughout this famed edition.
4328-two-expeditions-into-the-interior-o:
Charles Sturt wrote this first volume of his account of two expeditions into the interior of southern Australia, in the years 1828 to 1831. His subject is the search for the sources of the rivers, and his observations cover soil, climate, and the general resources of New South Wales. Sturt opens with a reflection on rivers and their causes.

Most men, he notes, watch a river only as it passes, in flood or drought, while the explorer must find its source and trace its feeders. The volume follows Sturt's parties inland, mapping water and country. It remains a foundation text of Australian exploration, written by the explorer himself.
4329-two-expeditions-into-the-interior-o:
Charles Sturt's second volume continues his account of the expeditions of 1828 to 1831 into the interior of southern Australia. It carries the search for the inland rivers further, with the same attention to soil, climate, and the resources of New South Wales. Sturt's opening image of the river returns: to know water, find its source.

The volume follows the parties through new country, with chapters on rivers, camps, and the peoples they met. Read after Volume I, it completes a journey that mapped much of the Murray-Darling basin. It remains essential reading for the history of Australian exploration, in the explorer's own words.
43427-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The Encyclopaedia Britannica, in its eleventh edition, was the most famous reference work in English. This volume carries the articles in the L range, running from Lord Chamberlain onward. Transcriber notes at the front list corrections made in articles on Lothair, on Pierre Loti, on Louis the Fourteenth, and on the town of Lugo.

The eleventh edition set a new mark for the signed article written by a named expert. Town entries give the hard facts of place, like the note that the bishopric of Lugo dates from a very early period. Lives of kings and writers stand a few pages from gazetteer entries on small Spanish towns. Louvet de Couvrai memoirs, written in hiding, picture the sufferings of the proscribed Girondists. One alphabet slice shows the whole method: history, place, and biography under one cover.
43517-bell-s-cathedrals-the-church-of-st:
Canon Routledge wrote an illustrated account of the church of Saint Martin at Canterbury, printed at London in 1898 for Bell's cathedral series. The south side of the church, from a photograph, fronts the book. Introduction and early Christianity in Britain open the chapters. The history of the church follows: Roman Canterbury, the Saxon invasion, and the mission of Saint Augustine.

The baptism of Ethelbert and the bishops of Saint Martin's close the history. A description of the church comes next, outside and in: dedication, walls, buttresses, doorways, font, the west wall of the nave, a Norman piscina, the chancel, and the chrismatory. Lists of rectors, the date of the church, and the eastern apse fill appendices. Queen Bertha's tomb and the chrismatory shut and open stand among the pictures. England's oldest church in use gets a loving record.
45626-history-of-company-k-of-the-140th-:
History of Company K holds the war tale of one Pennsylvania company. B Powelson, its first sergeant for past two years, wrote the book. A brevet captain of the unit led the work, with aid from its men. The book came out in Ohio in the year nineteen six.

The gift page sends the work to the dead and the living of the company. It praises grit, faith, and toil shown on long marches and hard fields. Peace work past the war is praised as part of the same true worth. Rolls, marches, and fight tales fill the rank and file war record. The book stands as a units own stone to its sons of the north.
45923-parasites-a-treatise-on-the-entozo:
Parasites is T Spencer Cobbold's treatise on the entozoa of man and animals. J and A Churchill published it in London in 1879. Cobbold dated his preface from 74 Portsdown Road in May 1879. The subtitle adds some account of the ectozoa, the external parasites. A synopsis of contents organises the worms by class. The book was the Victorian authority on its subject.

Section one treats the Trematoda, the flukes, from page 14. Section two takes the Cestoda, the tapeworms, at page 56. The Nematoda, roundworms and threadworms, follow at page 149. A fourth section turns to the thorny-headed worms. Cobbold wrote for medical men, veterinarians, and naturalists together. Human and animal hosts are treated side by side throughout. The treatise collects the species then known to infest both. Measurements in the text still use the old line, a twelfth of an inch. Bibliographies for each group support the descriptions.
51459-the-analysis-of-beauty-written-wit:
The Analysis of Beauty is a treatise by William Hogarth, the painter, printed at London in 1753 for the author and sold at his house in Leicester Fields. Its full title says it was written to fix the shifting ideas of taste. A verse from Milton about a curling, wanton train stands at the front, pointing to Hogarth's famous love of the wavy line.

In his preface Hogarth says beauty is seen and confessed by all, yet the cause of it has long been given up as too fine a matter to discuss. He warns that his work may upset long received views. As a man who never took up the pen before, he writes as a working artist, not a man of letters.
54593-adventures-of-an-aide-de-camp-or-a:
James Grant wrote a war tale of a young aide on a march in Calabria. Volume one came out in London in 1848. Grant also wrote The Romance of War. A Shakespeare line on love and war heads the book. Three books hold the whole tale of the young aide.

The landing in Calabria starts the march and the strife. A viscount, a hunchback named Truffi, and the Free Corps crowd in. The fight at Maida and a seized eagle mark the war path. Bianca D'Alfieri brings love to the camp tale. Nights with Gypsy folk add color twixt fights.
54594-adventures-of-an-aide-de-camp-or-a:
James Grant's tale of the Calabrian campaign continues in this second volume of three, printed in London by Smith, Elder and Company in 1848. An epigraph from Shakespeare stands at the head of the book.

The chapters move through Italian Intrigues in Country Quarters, Francatripa the Brigand, A Duel and a Discovery, The Siege of Scylla, and The Forlorn-Hope. Later chapters cover The Revolt of the Galley Slaves, The Cardinal, and the paired penitents, The First Penitent, The Nun, and The Second Penitent, The Cavalier. The volume opens by moonlight below the Villa Belcastro, where two great lynxes fight over the corpse of the Cavaliere Galdino and the riders force their horses past.
54595-adventures-of-an-aide-de-camp-or-a:
Adventures of an Aide-de-Camp is a novel by James Grant, issued in London in 1848. The hosted text is volume three of three. Its full title names the tale a campaign in Calabria. Grant was also the author of The Romance of War. The book opens with a passage from Shakespeare as its motto. The contents list runs to twenty-three chapters.

The closing volume moves through a chain of sieges and escapes. A villa is besieged, and a wedding follows. A tempest wrecks the ship Delight. French voltigeurs massacre men at Bagnara. A drum-head court-martial puts a life at risk. The hero is captured, then held in a bandit's cavern. The tale ends with the siege and fall of Scylla. Grant wrote from a soldier's knowledge of campaigning. His tales of the Napoleonic wars found many readers.
59673-the-life-or-legend-of-gaudama-the-:
The Life or Legend of Gaudama, volume two, tells the Burmese life of the Buddha, by Bishop Bigandet. Bigandet served as vicar apostolic of Ava and Pegu in Burma for Rome. Kegan Paul issued this fourth edition in London in nineteen twelve. The volume also treats the ways to Neibban and the Burmese monks, called phongyies.

Five long chapters carry the tale from the Buddha's old age to later councils. Chapter one shows him at seventy nine, preaching and crossing the Ganges by wonder. The deaths of his great followers Thariputra and Maukalan are told in turn. Chapter two gives his last meal, his sickness, and his death in a forest. Relics are split among kings, and a first council settles the teaching after him. A second council under King Kalathoka closes the long Burmese account.
63071-the-art-of-building-a-home-a-colle:
Barry Parker and Raymond Unwin, the architects of a new garden suburb age, gathered their lectures in this book. Longmans printed The Art of Building a Home in London in 1901. Parker writes the preface at the Quadrant, Buxton, in that year.

Two of his Building News pieces, reprinted long before, still drew letters, he says. Rather than reissue them stale, the partners chose a later, fuller word: lectures written for many audiences, with their sketches and photographs by them. Of the smaller middle class house opens the set, in Parker's own voice. Of the dignity of the home stands in the plan. Plain rooms, honest stuff, and air: the creed that would build Letchworth begins here.
64250-the-naturalist-in-vancouver-island:
The Naturalist in Vancouver Island and British Columbia is a book of wild lore by John Keast Lord. He was the lore man of a bound mark corps of the crown in the north west. The host text is the first of two parts. It was put out at London in eighteen sixty six. The front plate shows a group of the first folk of that land, drawn from a light print.

The first words sort the gap the book fills. Works past count treat those new lands, the hand says. They hold small lore of their wild life, if any. That lost link he dares in some part to give. But the book is not a book of wild lore a lone, he owns. He will not tire his reader with dull lists of kinds and breeds.
69274-chicago-and-the-old-northwest-1673:
Milo Milton Quaife, a history teacher in Chicago, wrote a study of Chicago and the old north west from 1673 to 1835, printed in October 1913. A front view shows Marquette at the Chicago portage, from a carving. Quaife states his aim as a study of how the north west frontier grew, with a history of Fort Dearborn.

Chapters run from the portage and Chicago in the sixteen hundreds through the Fox wars and the war for freedom. The founding of the fort, nine years of garrison life, and the battle and defeat in the war of 1812 follow. Added parts hold journals and reports from officers and a roll of one captains company.
9563-mabel-martin-a-harvest-idyl-and-oth:
Part four of Whittier's Narrative and Legendary Poems leads with Mabel Martin, a harvest idyll of witchcraft days. Susanna Martin of Amesbury was tried and hanged for witchcraft, the only woman hanged north of the Merrimac in that dread delusion. Mabel Martin tells her tale through harvest scenes: river valley, husking, a witch's daughter, and a betrothal. Other poems here include The Prophecy of Samuel Sewall and The Red River Voyageur.

Later pieces add The Preacher, The Truce of Piscataqua, and Cobbler Keezar's Vision, each a New England tale in verse. Whittier writes with pity for the accused and scorn for the panic. A reader gets a haunting set of colonial legends, where harvest joy meets a dark chapter of fear.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Robert Kerr opens his general history of voyages and travels with discovery from Alfred to Prince Henry. The first volume treats voyages from the ninth century to the fifteenth, then general voyages to the age of George the Third. A final part deduces the progress of navigation and commerce by sea and land. Kerr arranges the whole in systematic order with maps and charts.
a-volunteer-poilu: Henry Beston serves as a volunteer poilu in this memoir, dedicated from Topsfield in September 1916 to Professor Charles Townsend Copeland of Harvard. At Verdun he thought of Copeland and the friendly hearth of Hollis 15, far from a tragic city's empty, snow-swept streets. The contents follow the Rochambeau to war, loaded with ammunition and food. A dyestuffs agent, a machine lathes man, a Swede bound for the Foreign Legion, and a French officer's philosophy fill the voyage.
britannica-1911-bangweulu:
Bangweulu is a shallow lake of British Central Africa, formed by the head streams of the Congo. It lies high on a plateau, about 3,700 feet above the sea, in the north-west of a central basin. Streams drain into it from the south, east, and north, turning much of the ground into a morass of reeds and papyrus.

The name properly covers only the clear water, though it is sometimes used for the whole depression. Open water runs about sixty miles north to south and forty east to west. Long sandbanks nearly cut off the western pan, and islands dot the lake, the largest being Kirui on the east side. The 1911 Britannica entry maps this swampy basin in close geographic detail.
britannica-1911-cefalu:
Cefalu is a seaport and bishop's see in the province of Palermo, Sicily. It lies forty-two miles east of Palermo by rail. It had 13,273 people in 1901. The old town was called Cephaloedium. It was most likely of Sicel stock, in spite of its Greek name. The town takes its name from the headland it stood on, the Greek word for head. That rock rises 1,233 feet.

The old town's walls ran down to the shore in two long lines that guarded the port. Parts of a wall of huge squared blocks still stand at the modern Porta Garibaldi. The town does not show in the record before 396 BC. Its strength of site was the main source of its weight. On the hill stand the ruins of a small old structure in neat polygonal stonework. That style of building is very rare in Sicily.
britannica-1911-ormolu:
Ormolu, from French words for ground gold, is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a mix of copper and zinc. At times a bit of tin is added. The name is used as well for brass or copper with a gold coat. Its hue comes close to that of gold.

The hue can be raised in more than one way. A wash of gold varnish will do it. A dip in weak acid will do it too. A hard rub to a shine is a third way. The chief use of the stuff is for the mounts of fine home goods. With it the great French craft men of the seventeen hundreds won ends as fine as gold smith work. The mounts were cast first, then cut by hand.
britannica-1911-tulu: Tulu, also called Tuluva, is a tongue of the Dravidian family treated in a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was spoken chiefly in the South Kanara district of Madras, where most folk used it in daily life. Yet the entry notes that Tulu had no written works of its own and was not used for official business. In 1901 its speakers numbered more than half a million, so the piece records a widely spoken tongue that print and office work had left aside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cefalu:
Cefalu is a city on the northern coast of Sicily, in the province of Palermo, and the seat of a diocese suffragan to Palermo. Destroyers from Messina leveled it, and King Roger I rebuilt it about 1130. Its first bishop, Nicetas, attended the Eighth General Council at Constantinople in 869 for the trial of Photius. Tocelmo held the see when Roger rebuilt the city.

Later bishops include Arduino II, exiled twice for opposing Frederick II. Nicolò died in 1352 while held at Castel Grassario. Fra Francesco of the house of Gonzaga founded the first seminary opened in Sicily. Roger's cathedral, often restored, remains a fine monument of Norman architecture, and the diocese counted 22 parishes and 160,320 inhabitants.
christopher-columbus-and-the-new-world-o:
Preparations at Palos fill Volume 2 of Filson Young's Christopher Columbus and the New World of His Discovery, his 1906 life of the Admiral. The ships ride the mud banks of the Tinto at low water while caulkers refit them for the Atlantic. Gomaz Rascon and Christoval Quintero, unwilling owners of the pressed Pinta, quietly sabotage gear and seams. Columbus fights delay and ridicule with the departure date finally fixed.

Young writes the fitting-out as a study of the Admiral's persistence: every missing rope is an argument against his idea, answered in person. Letters home, including a farewell to a William, show the private man under the public visionary. The volume carries the fleet from parchment grants to salt water. Readers following Young get the unglamorous truth here: the first voyage was won in dockyards before it was won at sea.
doe-osti-2997579-de-novo-synthesis-and-n:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory abbreviated final report LLNL-TR-2012019, by Sankar Narayanasamy and Abisola Abisoye-Ogunniyan, dated October 2025, covers building a human immune receptor in the laboratory for imaging. The receptor is TLR4, the cell-surface sensor that recognizes bacterial lipopolysaccharide and sounds the alarm. Seeing its full shape at near-atomic detail has been blocked by how hard it is to produce intact.

The team produced TLR4 bound to a nanolipoprotein particle using a cell-based method, keeping all three parts together: the outer sensing domain, the membrane span, and the inner signaling domain. The protein stayed functional and suited time-resolved single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, which freezes many copies and averages their images. Structural biologists gain a route to watch this receptor work, step by step, in its native-like setting.
doe-osti-3028498-nuclear-power-plant-inf:
Steven J Maheras and Miriam Juckett of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Virgil O Peoples of Idaho National Laboratory, and colleagues from the Federal Railroad Administration. They evaluated the Duane Arnold nuclear plant in Iowa as Supplement 22 to report PNNL-35730, dated March 21, 2026. The series inspects shut-down reactor sites one by one: what rail, road, and lifting infrastructure exists for eventually shipping the site's used nuclear fuel away.

The evaluation was prepared for the Energy Department's Office of Storage and Transportation. Acronym tables name the local railroads, Canadian National and the Iowa Northern Railway, and the site's independent spent fuel storage installation. The authors include the series' standing caution: the work is technical support for future decisions and does not override the Standard Contract that governs the government's fuel obligations.
doe-osti-3028501-nuclear-power-plant-inf:
Steven J Maheras, Miriam Juckett, Virgil O Peoples, and colleagues. They evaluated Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania as Supplement 21 to report PNNL-35730, dated March 21, 2026, for the Energy Department's Office of Storage and Transportation. The series documents what infrastructure each shut-down plant site offers for the eventual removal of its used nuclear fuel. Three Mile Island carries a history no other site in the series shares.

Unit 1, an 819 megawatt electric pressurized water reactor, began operating in 1974 and shut down in 2019, and all its used fuel has left the spent fuel pool. The fuel now sits in 46 TSC-37 dry storage canisters in a MAGNASTOR system. Owner Constellation has weighed restarting the unit, and in May 2025 the site was renamed the Christopher M Crane Clean Energy Center. The evaluation records these facts because they change the shipping picture.
doe-osti-3362628-oil-filled-flow-shield-:
Emma D. Cotter, Spencer P. Nelson, Joseph H. Haxel, and colleagues at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory test a quieter underwater ear in this March 2026 report, with XFlow Energy staff sharing the work. Hydrophones in rivers and tidal channels suffer flow noise: turbulence past the sensor masks low sounds. An oil-filled flow shield wraps the sensor to calm that noise. Field trials pitted a shielded hydrophone against a bare one, side by side in moving water.

Peak flows hit 0.75 meters per second. Below 200 hertz, the bare sensor noise climbed with flow speed, while the shielded sensor held nearly flat. A tone near 60 hertz, barely visible to the bare unit, stood out clearly behind the shield. Results were binned across bands from 20 to 50 hertz up to 4,000 to 5,000 hertz.
doe-osti-3365409-process-development-and:
A CRADA final report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, LBNL-2001764, dated May 27, 2026, with Deepti Tanjore as technical contact, closes a scale-up project with Zymergen on fermentation-made molecules. The product was histamine, made by genetically modified brewer's yeast fed on dextrose. Zymergen's one-liter work had reached 0.9 grams per liter; Berkeley Lab's process development unit took the strain to production-relevant scale.

Two bench campaigns in 2-liter reactors tuned glucose feed, vitamins, and inoculum, reaching 2.41 grams per liter. The chosen recipe then ran at 300 liters and hit 3.57 grams per liter, the project's best, yielding 980.5 grams of histamine in 235.8 liters of clarified broth at 98 percent mass balance. The report notes drily that the partner company no longer exists.
doe-osti-3374899-t3tris-ai-driven-invers:
Los Alamos National Laboratory capability snapshot LA-UR-26-25126, issued June 19, 2026, by Dharmesh N. Patel, presents T3tris, a generative AI tool for designing cellular materials in reverse.
